rv.q: It will delight a broad audience, and even those resistant to the unashamedly corny will likely be won over by the breathtaking look and strident performances in this feat of spectacle and seduction.
So the second half mixes its spectacle and its sadness to winning effect.
In performance this Gatsby turns out to be a sleek, ravishingly designed ocean liner of a show, with enough musical oomph and vocal power to distract you from the hollowness at its heart.
But while it may not fully engage one's emotions, this is a Show with a capital S.
There’s little of the chilly majesty of the book in this show, but there are a lot of very pretty sequins.
If you’re in the market for a generic but gorgeous-looking musical romance with a Great Gatsby theme… then this will do, I suppose.
By the time the revellers return for a reprise of Roaring On, the champagne has lost its sparkle.

Instead, we get a screechy clodhopping musical that amps up the Roaring Twenties clichés at the expense of anything Fitzgerald had to say about class, money and the scissoring chasms between appearances and reality.
Fresh from Broadway, this production encapsulates the worst of peacockingly splashy entertainment – the kind whose soul has been suctioned out in the making.
This Great Gatsby is a visually stunning, emotionally resonant, and thoroughly entertaining production.
Even as disaster strikes, this spectacular party never ends.
Two and a half hours of tedious hoofing and banal glamour, a band and singer entertaining the freeloaders all the way to hell, a foghorn the metaphor that opens the show.
But if you’re devoted to the spirit of F Scott Fitzgerald’s original, this will leave you with mixed feelings.

The Great Gatsby isn't a great tuner: it's neither cynical enough to really explore the dark underbelly of the F Scott Fitzgerald story with which it flirts, nor is it distinguished enough to provide the uplift of musical theatre at its best, but it's the epitome of a slick, escapist West End night out.

Ultimately, the production feels like big Broadway, by numbers and it would be remiss of me to gloss over the hot interval conversation topic, namely that many of the show’s tunes seem to borrow key refrains from elsewhere.
It’s serviceable but there’s no wow factor.
The show is high on visual opulence, but low on heart and soul.
Big, beautiful and bold, The Great Gatsby isn’t just a good show, it’s great.
Fortunately, more than any other production I’ve ever seen, The Great Gatsby: A New Musical is big enough, bold enough and spectacular enough to fit right in.
Marc Bruni's capable direction does deliver a depiction of heartless opportunism in an America booming into a consumerist powerhouse.
The Great Gatsby at the London Coliseum is a triumph of style over substance.

cn.t: A visually dazzling spectacle with stunning Art Deco design and strong performances, but critics find it sacrifices the novel's subtlety and depth for Broadway razzle-dazzle, resulting in a hollow, crowd-pleasing adaptation that prioritizes style over substance.
